b: Thanksgiving is supposed to be about gratitude and togetherness. We travel long distances, spend hours preparing meals, and gather around tables with people we love. We might even take a moment to express appreciation in honor of the holiday. But feeling connected can be more complicated than simply being together.

Sometimes we find ourselves sitting across from people we’ve known our entire lives, struggling to think of something to talk about. We ask the same familiar questions, tell the same stories, or carefully steer clear of subjects that might spark an argument.
And sometimes, even surrounded by family, we feel surprisingly lonely.

The good news is that meaningful connection doesn’t require a deep conversation, a dramatic revelation, or a perfectly harmonious family. Drs. John and Julie Gottman’s work reminds us that romantic relationships are strengthened through everyday moments of turning toward one another. A question, a shared laugh, or a thoughtful follow-up can communicate something powerful: I see you. I’m interested in you. You matter to me.

Of course, these same concepts can be applied to non-romantic, familial relationships. Not everyone feels comfortable having heartfelt conversations about gratitude, fondness, and appreciation, especially around the Thanksgiving table. Some family members love to go deep, while others would rather keep things light and playful. And that’s okay!

The goal isn’t to force meaningful conversations but to create opportunities for fun and interesting conversations. By asking questions you don’t already know the answers to, you can find a comfortable middle ground between boring small talk and conversations that feel overly intense or emotionally charged.
How to Gamify the Thanksgiving Table
One way to take the pressure off is to make a game out of these ideas by playing this game this Thanksgiving. Sometimes a little playfulness is all it takes.
Instructions: Print out the following list of ten questions and pass it around the table. Each person is invited to choose a question, and then answer it.
(No pressure, no right or wrong answers, and everyone is welcome to pass.)
What’s one thing someone at this table does that you appreciate?
What’s something you’re more grateful for now than you were ten years ago?
What’s a little thing someone did for you recently that made your day better?
What’s something you’re looking forward to?
What’s a fond memory of someone who isn’t able to be here today.
What’s something about our family or our traditions that you particularly enjoy?
What are you most excited about for the coming year?
What are you reading, watching, or listening to lately that you find really interesting?
What hobby have you been spending your time on lately?
These are just a starting point. Feel free to make up your own questions, especially ones that fit your family’s personality and sense of humor.
The Real Magic Happens After the Question
Here’s something important to remember: Asking a good question is only the beginning. What you do with the answer matters even more.

In Gottman Method Couples Therapy, we talk about bids for connection. A bid is any attempt to connect with someone by showing genuine interest, affection or concern. It might be as obvious as offering a hug or as subtle as sharing something interesting that happened during the day.

When someone answers one of these Thanksgiving questions, they’re offering you a little glimpse into their world. How you respond can either encourage them to share more or bring the conversation to a halt.
Imagine your uncle mentions that he’s been learning to play the guitar.
You could respond with a quick “That’s nice” and move on to the next question.
Or you could turn toward him with genuine curiosity:
“Really? What made you decide to start?”

Notice that you don’t have to be interested in playing the guitar yourself. You’re showing interest in him. That’s what turning toward looks like in everyday life. And it doesn’t require a long conversation. Sometimes a smile, a laugh, or a simple “Tell me more about that” is enough to help someone feel seen and valued.
Small Moments Can Make a Big Difference
As you gather around the table this Thanksgiving, remember that you don’t have to create a picture-perfect holiday to create meaningful memories.

Not every conversation will go smoothly. Someone might give a one-word answer. Someone else might change the subject, or your family might not want to play this game at all. That’s okay, it still gives you an opportunity to apply these ideas in a more spontaneous manner.
